headline_en: Target of sending 10 million workers in 5 years: how ready is our skills training
summary_en: The Bangladesh government has set a target of placing 10 million workers abroad in five years, but an additional secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry said current capacity to reach it is 55 to 60 percent. The article lists the government training network (110 institutions, 55 courses), the BOESL sending figures for fiscal 2025-26 and the launch of the Overseas Employment Platform (OEP). Officials and experts say demand for unskilled workers abroad is shrinking and Bangladeshi certificates lack international recognition.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh government has set a target of employing a total of 10 million (1 crore) workers abroad over the next five years; reaching it would require sending at least 2 million (20 lakh) workers abroad a year on average.

Bangladesh has 110 active government technical training institutions: 104 Technical Training Centres (TTC) and 6 Institutes of Marine Technology. They run 55 training courses of various durations and give technical certificates to more than 1.2 million (12 lakh) people a year.

At a national consultation organised in Dhaka by Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP) on 28 September, Saiful Haque Chowdhury, additional secretary of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, said Bangladesh's current capacity to reach the target of sending 10 million workers abroad in five years is 55 to 60 percent.
facts.source_in_article: Saiful Haque Chowdhury, additional secretary, expatriates' welfare ministry

facts.statement: Mokhlesur Rahman Akand, joint secretary of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, said the market for unskilled workers abroad is steadily shrinking and that it is now nearly impossible to get work in foreign labour markets without skills. The article says opportunities for unskilled workers are falling and demand for skilled workers is rising in newer developed markets such as Japan and Europe.
facts.source_in_article: Mokhlesur Rahman Akand, joint secretary, expatriates' welfare ministry

facts.statement: A 'Japan Cell' ('Japani Cell') has been formed in the expatriates' welfare ministry to coordinate work related to employment in Japan.
facts.source_in_article: Mokhlesur Rahman Akand, joint secretary, expatriates' welfare ministry

facts.statement: In July 2026 expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told parliament that forecasts of potential global demand for about 11.5 million (1 crore 15 lakh) workers had been collected through Bangladesh missions abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament

facts.statement: More than 700,000 (7 lakh) workers have received certificates at over 2,300 institutions under the National Skills Development Authority (NSDA), but international recognition of these certificates in the global market remains a major challenge; foreign employers' specific demands are not fully matched with the domestic training curriculum.

State-owned Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) sent 19,197 workers abroad in fiscal year 2025-26, the highest in its history: 14,543 to Jordan (the most), 1,812 to Brunei and 1,404 to South Korea.

A technology-based 'Overseas Employment Platform' (OEP) has been launched, bringing foreign employers, candidates, training centres and Bangladesh embassies onto one platform for visa verification and transparency in recruitment.

Employment experts say separate training programmes under different ministries should be brought under one common government certificate and raised to international standard, and trained workers should be linked directly to foreign jobs through government and private recruitment systems.

headline_en: Qatar wants to take workers in four more sectors
summary_en: At the seventh Bangladesh-Qatar joint committee meeting in Dhaka on 18 May 2026, Qatar's labour minister expressed interest in taking Bangladeshi electricians, plumbers, AC technicians and welders trained at five specified Technical Training Centres. Bangladesh asked Qatar to open visa and medical centres in all eight divisional cities because there is only one in Dhaka. Figures on Bangladeshis in Qatar were given by both ministers.

facts.statement: At the seventh Bangladesh-Qatar joint committee meeting on Monday 18 May 2026, held in the expatriates' welfare ministry's meeting room in Dhaka, Qatar expressed interest in taking workers in four new sectors besides the existing ones: electricians, plumbers, AC technicians and welding.
Qatar will take workers trained at five specified Technical Training Centres (TTC) in Bangladesh; the article does not name the five centres.

Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said more than 400,000 (4 lakh) Bangladeshi workers are currently in Qatar and that 107,598 Bangladeshi workers went to Qatar in 2023; he hoped Qatar would take double that number in 2026.
Qatar's labour minister Ali bin Samikh Al Marri said about 473,000 Bangladeshi workers are currently working in Qatar, 30 percent of them in the development sector and the rest in other occupations.
facts.source_in_article: Qatar labour minister Ali bin Samikh Al Marri

facts.statement: For Qatar-bound workers there is currently only one Qatar visa and medical centre in Bangladesh, in Dhaka, which the ministry calls inadequate. The Bangladeshi minister asked Qatar to set up visa centres and medical centres in the eight divisional cities; Qatar's labour minister said he would personally request Qatar's interior minister to implement this.
Qatar's labour minister said two special training centres have already been set up in Qatar to turn unskilled workers into skilled ones.
facts.source_in_article: Qatar labour minister Ali bin Samikh Al Marri

facts.statement: The minister said 110 technical training centres under the expatriates' welfare ministry give training in 55 trades related to overseas employment.

State minister for expatriates' welfare Md. Nurul Haque asked Qatar's labour minister to recruit skilled Bangladeshi doctors, engineers, nurses, caregivers, imams, muezzins, khatibs and religious teachers.

headline_en: Now is the time to build alternative labour markets (editorial)
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial says the Middle East war has exposed Bangladesh's dependence on a few Gulf labour markets: BMET clearances in the first 10 days of March 2026 fell by about 50 percent year on year and several hundred flights from Dhaka were cancelled. It notes Malaysia has been closed since June 2024, warns of rising irregular sea migration to Europe and of rackets recruiting for Russia, and calls for investment in skills and language training.

facts.statement: According to BMET, the number of workers taking clearance to go abroad in the first 10 days of March 2026 fell by about 50 percent compared with the same period a year earlier.

After the war began, the airspace of several Middle Eastern countries was closed and several hundred flights from Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport were cancelled; many workers could not leave and many who had come home on leave were stranded in Bangladesh.
In 2025, 67 percent of all Bangladeshi workers who went abroad went to Saudi Arabia, and about 90 percent went to just five countries, although the list of sending destinations has 168 countries.
Between 4.5 and 5 million (45 to 50 lakh) Bangladeshis work in the Middle East; reports of several expatriate Bangladeshis dying in the war situation had already arrived by late March 2026.

The Bangladesh government opened a hotline and control room to help expatriates affected by the Middle East war (numbers not printed) and is contacting the countries concerned to extend the visa validity of stranded workers.
Malaysia's labour market has been closed to Bangladeshi workers since June 2024 over allegations of irregularities and a syndicate, and was still closed in late March 2026.
Dishonest rackets have become active around Russia as a new market, collecting workers with the lure of good wages or citizenship.
The tendency to go to Europe by sea is rising; research organisations warn that with regular migration paths narrowing, many may try dangerous routes lured by broker rings.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial citing research organisations

facts.statement: Bangladesh has signed agreements with several countries including Italy, Japan and South Korea as new labour markets; these markets require specific skills, training and language ability, which Bangladesh lacks.

headline_en: Agreement signed with Saudi Arabia on worker recruitment
summary_en: On 6 October 2025 in Riyadh, Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia signed the first formal agreement on recruitment of general workers in 50 years of diplomatic relations. Before the signing, adviser Asif Nazrul raised correct employment contracts, employers' duty to renew the iqama and quick exit visas for workers who want to go home. A former BAIRA secretary general said an agreement, unlike an MoU, is legally binding and lets the government go to court for a worker.

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia signed an agreement on worker recruitment in Riyadh on Monday 6 October 2025, the first formal agreement on recruitment of general workers in the two countries' 50 years of diplomatic relations. It was signed by expatriates' welfare adviser Professor Asif Nazrul and Saudi Minister of Human Resources and Social Development Engineer Ahmed bin Sulaiman Al-Rajhi.

Recruitment of Bangladeshi workers to Saudi Arabia began informally in 1976 with no formal general-worker agreement; two special agreements were signed earlier, on domestic worker recruitment in 2015 and on skill verification in 2022.

In the bilateral meeting before the signing, adviser Asif Nazrul asked that employment contracts in Saudi Arabia be correct, that employers carry out the responsibility of renewing the iqama (the legal work permit), and that workers who wish to return home get an 'exit' visa quickly. The Saudi minister instructed those concerned to take effective steps to resolve these quickly.

Ali Haider Chowdhury, former secretary general of BAIRA (the recruiting agency owners' association), said workers are usually sent under a memorandum of understanding, which has no legal obligation; the agreement creates legal protection for workers sent to Saudi Arabia and the government can now go to court on a worker's behalf if needed.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury, former BAIRA secretary general

headline_en: 23 organisations demand transparent sending of workers to Malaysia
summary_en: Bangladesh Civil Society for Migrants (BCSM), a platform of 23 organisations, issued a joint statement on Tuesday 12 August 2025 expressing concern at reports that people linked to the Malaysia labour-market syndicate are being cleared and that Bangladesh agreed to Malaysia's request to suspend the investigation. BCSM demanded trial of those involved, a re-investigation and judicial inquiry, and open, transparent sending of workers. The statement says workers were charged five to six times the government-set cost in 2022-2024.

facts.statement: According to the government's white paper on the economy, media reports and ACC complaints cited by BCSM, each worker sent to Malaysia in 2022, 2023 and 2024 was charged five to six times the government-set cost, with corruption of several thousand crore taka involving syndicates in both Malaysia and Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: BCSM joint statement citing the white paper on the economy, media and the ACC

facts.statement: BCSM said reports had been published that the family of former MP 'Lotus Kamal' (former finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal) and three former MPs linked to the Malaysia syndicate were being cleared of the allegations.

Malaysian outlet Malaysiakini recently reported that Bangladesh agreed to Malaysia's request to suspend the investigation of allegations against the influential syndicate involved in exploiting Malaysia-bound Bangladeshi migrant workers.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysiakini, as cited in the BCSM statement

facts.statement: BCSM demanded no impunity for those involved in the Malaysia syndicate, a re-investigation and a judicial inquiry, public disclosure of progress on the Anti-Corruption Commission's complaint, and that those involved not be allowed into the new sending process.
facts.source_in_article: BCSM joint statement signed by chair Tasneem Siddiqui and co-chair Syed Saiful Haque

facts.statement: In 2017 and 2018 there was a syndicate of ten in sending workers to Malaysia; BCSM says those involved in the irregularities were never tried.
The Chief Adviser visited Malaysia on 11 to 13 August 2025 in the context of reopening the Malaysian labour market; BCSM urged that eliminating the syndicate not lose importance.

The 23 BCSM member organisations include RMMRU, WARBE Development Foundation, BRAC, OKUP, BASTOB, Ain o Salish Kendra, BASUG, Rights Jessore, INAFI, Manusher Jonno Foundation, BOMSA, IMA Research Foundation, BCWWF, YPSA, BOAF, DevCom Limited, Films 4 Peace Foundation, Change Makers, ACD, CCDA, Karmojibi Nari, BILS and BNSK.

headline_en: New advisers' committee to recommend on 9 matters including expanding labour markets abroad
summary_en: On Sunday 15 June 2025 the Cabinet Division issued a notification forming an 11-member advisers' council committee on overseas recruitment of Bangladeshis, convened by adviser Asif Nazrul, replacing the 8 April 2024 notification with identical terms of reference. The article gives BMET figures showing overseas employment fell by 300,000 in 2024 because Malaysia, the UAE and Oman were closed, with only Saudi Arabia remaining among the big markets.

facts.statement: On Sunday 15 June 2025 the Cabinet Division issued a notification forming the 11-member 'Advisers' Council Committee on Recruitment of Bangladeshis Abroad', convened by expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul; the same notification cancelled the notification of 8 April 2024. The previous government's committee had 13 members. The expatriates' welfare ministry gives it secretarial support.

The committee's terms of reference cover nine matters including coordinating overseas manpower recruitment, guidance on expanding labour markets and finding new ones, tackling overseas employment challenges, overall welfare of migrant workers, skills development of aspiring migrants and sending remittances through legal channels; the text is identical to the 2024 terms.
BMET figures: 617,000 workers went abroad in 2021, more than 1.1 million in 2022, 1.3 million in 2023 and 1 million in 2024, a fall of 300,000 from 2023.

As of June 2025 three labour markets, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates and Oman, were closed to Bangladeshi workers; among the big markets only Saudi Arabia remained. Malaysia has been closed since June 2024.
In 2024, 90 percent of Bangladeshi workers who went abroad went to five countries: Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Qatar, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates.
More than 125,000 (over one and a quarter lakh) Bangladeshi workers went to Oman in 2023, but only 358 in 2024.
About 100,000 Bangladeshi workers went to the United Arab Emirates in 2023 and 47,000, less than half, in 2024.
About 500,000 Bangladeshi workers went to Saudi Arabia in 2023 and about 625,000 (six and a quarter lakh) in 2024; Saudi Arabia was the only country that received more than 100,000 workers in 2024.

Although the government claims to send workers to 168 countries, workers went to 135 countries in 2024, most in token numbers: 14 countries received one worker each, 14 received two each, and 8 countries received 10,000 workers.

headline_en: No irregularity or discrimination in the process of sending workers to Malaysia: Lutfey Siddiqi
summary_en: After the opening session of the Bangladesh-Malaysia joint working group meeting at the InterContinental hotel in Dhaka on 21 May 2025, the Chief Adviser's special envoy Lutfey Siddiqi said transparency would be ensured in sending workers to Malaysia. He said about 8,000 workers who completed all steps but could not go when the market closed in 2024 would go first, through BOESL under government management, and that Malaysia wants to take workers through a limited number of agencies.

facts.statement: A Bangladesh-Malaysia joint working group meeting on sending Bangladeshi workers opened on Wednesday 21 May 2025 at the InterContinental hotel in Dhaka; the process for sending workers to Malaysia was due to be finalised at it. Malaysia's seven-member delegation was led by M. Shahrin bin Umar, deputy secretary general of Malaysia's Ministry of Human Resources.

Lutfey Siddiqi, the Chief Adviser's special envoy on international affairs, said about 8,000 workers who had completed all procedures but could not go to Malaysia because the market closed in 2024 will go in the first phase, sent quickly through BOESL under government management.
facts.source_in_article: Lutfey Siddiqi, Chief Adviser's special envoy

facts.statement: Lutfey Siddiqi said that because Bangladesh has a large number of recruiting agencies, the Malaysian government is interested in taking workers through a limited number of recruiting agencies; the joint working group would discuss amending the memorandum of understanding if needed to keep transparency.
facts.source_in_article: Lutfey Siddiqi, Chief Adviser's special envoy

facts.statement: Lutfey Siddiqi said Malaysia set no conditions on the labour market issue, including no condition to withdraw cases against those who formed the past syndicate, and that the Malaysian government was holding inter-ministerial meetings on giving multiple-entry visas to Bangladeshi workers.

headline_en: 23 migrant organisations do not want old experience repeated in sending workers to Malaysia
summary_en: On Wednesday 14 May 2025 Bangladesh Civil Society for Migrants (BCSM), a platform of 23 organisations including RMMRU and BRAC, sent recommendations to the interim government on the Malaysian labour market that was about to reopen after about a year. It says the 2021 MoU gave Malaysia the power to select agencies, which produced a syndicate that pushed the cost of going to BDT 550,000, and some workers found no job on arrival. It asks that Bangladesh be treated like Malaysia's 14 other source countries.

facts.statement: The memorandum of understanding signed with Malaysia in 2021 for sending workers gave Malaysia the responsibility of selecting agencies; BCSM says this led a Malaysian company and some Bangladeshi agencies to form a syndicate.
BCSM says that because of the syndicate the cost of sending a worker to Malaysia rose to BDT 550,000 (five and a half lakh taka).

BCSM says that earlier not all job appointment letters for Malaysia were proper: some workers got no job after arriving, and many lived jobless abroad half-fed or unfed, or survived on money brought from home.

Before the syndicate was created, some Malaysian companies recruited workers from Bangladesh at the employer's cost; BCSM says they can no longer take workers, and that the syndicate's illegal fee system deprives Bangladeshi workers of decent work.
As of mid-May 2025 the Malaysian labour market was about to reopen after being closed for about a year; a delegation led by expatriates' welfare adviser Professor Asif Nazrul was in Malaysia.

BCSM recommended that the delegation's main goal be to persuade Malaysia to take workers from Bangladesh by the same process it uses for its 14 other source countries, to cut costs and secure assurance of jobs on arrival, to send a letter to Malaysia's prime minister to drop one clause of the MoU, and for all ministries together to break up the syndicate.

BCSM says the Malaysian market has been unstable for 20 years, opening and closing repeatedly because of mismanagement in both countries, and that no irregularity has ever occurred in sending workers to Korea and Japan.

headline_en: High Court orders progress report on action against mismanagement to be filed on 27 August
summary_en: On Sunday 27 April 2025 a High Court bench ordered a progress report by 27 August on action taken over the 17,777 workers who held BMET clearance cards but could not go to Malaysia before the market closed on 31 May 2024. The ministry's inquiry report puts the blame entirely on the recruiting agencies and recommends legal action, immediate refunds and settlement of complaints of charging above the ministry's maximum migration cost of BDT 78,990. The government side said those who could not go would be taken to Malaysia on a priority basis.

facts.statement: On Sunday 27 April 2025 a High Court bench of Justice Fahmida Quader and Justice Mubina Asaf ordered that a report on progress of action against mismanagement in workers' travel to Malaysia after final clearance be filed in court on 27 August 2025.

The ministry inquiry report says 17,777 workers could not go to Malaysia after BMET issued their clearance cards, which is 3.66 percent of workers who received BMET clearance cards; responsibility for the failure lies entirely with the recruiting agencies concerned.
facts.source_in_article: Inquiry committee report of the expatriates' welfare ministry

facts.statement: Malaysia allotted Bangladesh a total quota of 532,162 workers; sending against this quota began in August 2022 and ran until 31 May 2024.

In that period the ministry gave recruitment permission for 527,999 workers, but recruiting agencies collected BMET smart cards for 493,729; agencies did not apply to BMET for smart cards for 34,270 workers despite having recruitment permission, which the report calls clear negligence by the agencies.
facts.source_in_article: Inquiry committee report, from the BMET database

facts.statement: The maximum migration cost for Malaysia set by the expatriates' welfare ministry was BDT 78,990.
facts.source_in_article: Inquiry committee report; lawyer Tanvir Ahmed

facts.statement: The inquiry report recommends legal action against the recruiting agencies for failure and neglect of duty, directing the agencies to immediately refund money taken from workers who could not go, and lawful settlement of complaints that agencies took more than the ministry-set maximum of BDT 78,990.

The expatriates' welfare ministry formed a six-member committee on 2 June 2024 to find why workers could not be sent to Malaysia. Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed filed a writ on 3 June 2024; on 16 July 2024 the High Court issued a rule and interim order requiring an updated report every six months on action against the mismanagement.

The court asked what action was taken against the agencies and what was done to refund all money to those charged more than the set BDT 78,990. The government side said those who could not go will be taken to Malaysia on a priority basis, and must report what steps were taken.

On 2 June 2024 a daily ran a report headlined '20,000 crore taka looted, breaking the dreams of 30,000 youths' on the Malaysian labour market, and an English daily the same day reported that more than 3,000 workers did not get tickets because of mismanagement.
facts.source_in_article: Newspaper reports attached to the writ

headline_en: Return my husband before he dies, pleads wife of a migrant in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: Mizanur Rahman, 62, from Noakhali, has worked in Saudi Arabia since 1993, has been undocumented since 2017 and has lain paralysed in Jubail General Hospital since a stroke on 28 February 2025. His wife Nasrin Akter got no solution from the Bangladesh embassy, which says an employer's compensation case must be settled first, and applied to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board on 9 April with help from BRAC's migration programme. The Board cannot directly help undocumented workers and forwarded the application to the ministry, which wrote to the embassy's labour wing on 16 April.

facts.statement: Under Saudi law a worker has no scope to work for anyone other than the kafeel (employer); working for someone else needs the kafeel's permission, and a worker who breaks this becomes illegal.

Mizanur Rahman (62) of Noakhali, in Saudi Arabia since 1993 and last home on leave in 2015, had a stroke on 28 February 2025 and was admitted to Jubail General Hospital after the Saudi state emergency number was called; one side of his body is paralysed and he cannot return on his own.

The Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia told the family it would arrange to send Mizanur home once the compensation case filed against him by his employer is resolved; the employer has since died but the case remains.

Wage Earners' Welfare Board sources say the Board cannot directly help migrant workers who are illegal (undocumented); it therefore forwarded Nasrin's application to the expatriates' welfare ministry.

Nasrin applied to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board on 9 April 2025, with help from BRAC's migration programme, and made the same application to the ministry. On 16 April the expatriates' welfare ministry wrote to the labour wing of the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia requesting urgent arrangements to send the sick migrant home.
Wage Earners' Welfare Board director general Md. Golam Sarwar Bhuiyan said whatever is needed to bring Mizanur home would be done and instructions for quick action had been given.

headline_en: Two young men from Madaripur drown in the Mediterranean on the way to Italy
summary_en: Suman Hawlader (22) and Nasir Matubbar (30) of Rajoir, Madaripur died on 4 March 2025 when the engine of their boat caught fire in the Mediterranean off Libya on the way to Italy. Brokers took them from Dhaka via Dubai to Libya; relatives say brokers Arif Molla of Rajoir and Dipu of Naogaon took about BDT 35 lakh from the two families. At least 16 people from Madaripur district have died on this route in 2025.

facts.statement: Suman Hawlader (22) of Char Mostafapur village, Badarpasha union, and Nasir Matubbar (30) of Shakharpar, both in Rajoir upazila, Madaripur, died on 4 March 2025 when the engine of the motorised boat carrying them and others (10 youths in all) from Libya towards Italy caught fire in the Mediterranean and many jumped into the sea; their families learned of the deaths on the night of Sunday 9 March.
The two left home on 8 February 2025; the broker ring took them from Dhaka via Dubai to Libya, and they set off by engine boat for Italy on 4 March.

Relatives say Arif Molla (son of Ali Molla of Shakharpar, Rajoir), a member of a human trafficking ring, and a broker named Dipu from Naogaon district took about BDT 35 lakh from the families of Suman and Nasir on the promise of taking them to Italy. Suman's father says he sold land and borrowed to pay.

Arif Molla's uncle and neighbour Md. Rashed Hawlader said Arif is currently in Libya and his father Ali Molla has taken 20 to 25 people to Italy so far; Arif was not found at home and his phone was off, and the family's own broker stopped answering calls.

facts.statement: Rajoir police station officer-in-charge Mohammad Masud Khan said legal action would be taken if the families file a written complaint against the brokers.
Madaripur district court lawyer Sujan Bhowmik said local brokers get caught but the ringleaders stay in Libya, Italy and elsewhere and are never arrested, which is why the crime does not fall.
At least 16 people from Madaripur district died in 2025 on the way to Italy illegally, including 10 young men from Rajoir upazila and 1 from Sadar upazila who died on 24 January 2025.

headline_en: Some proposals to end mismanagement in labour migration (column)
summary_en: In a column, Dhaka University professor and RMMRU founding chair Tasneem Siddiqui sets out eight proposals for the new interim government on migration governance: budget, voting rights for migrants, safety for women migrants, syndicate-free recruitment, a specialised cadre, stronger institutions, skills and remittance policy. She cites RMMRU research that 19 percent of migrants paid part or all of the cost but could not go, and another 31 percent faced harassment after going.

facts.statement: RMMRU research found that 19 percent of migrants could not go abroad even after paying part or all of the migration cost, and another 31 percent suffered various kinds of harassment after going abroad; some had to return quickly without work or wages, and some endured physical and mental abuse.
facts.source_in_article: RMMRU research, cited by Tasneem Siddiqui

facts.statement: The column says a portion of women migrant workers suffered sexual harassment in addition to other fraud, and many returned dead.

Tasneem Siddiqui proposes ending the rule under which individually obtained visas are processed through recruiting agencies and strengthening DEMO offices instead, forcing recruiting agencies to source good-quality company visas, and making sub-agents' informal services part of the formal process.

For women migrants the column calls for ending modern slavery in women's migration, legal aid and psychosocial services for abused and dismissed women migrants, safe homes in destination countries, and care for children born of sexual abuse.

Civil society organisations have long demanded that at least 1 percent of the revenue budget, or an amount equal to 5 percent of annual remittances, be spent on protecting the rights of and serving workers and their families; the expatriates' welfare ministry's budget remains among the lowest of all ministries.
Long-term and short-term Bangladeshi migrants have long sought the chance to vote; the Election Commission has discussed it at various times but not implemented it.

The column lists reasons for falling or slowing formal remittances: inflation, the exchange-rate gap between formal and informal channels, the high cost of sending, distrust of the banking sector, traders' under-invoicing because of unfair tax policy, and recruiting agencies' need for money abroad to buy visas.

The expatriates' welfare ministry was created by the newly elected government in light of the 'National Strategy on Streamlining Labour Recruitment 2001' prepared by the then caretaker government; migration was declared a 'thrust sector' of the economy by about 2009.

The column says the national skills policy does not include international migrants, and that expatriates' welfare ministry officials are transferred under general civil service rules after a few years, so it proposes a dedicated 'cadre service' and an evaluation of BMET, DEMO, TTC, BOESL and Probashi Kallyan Bank.

headline_en: Technology is raising the risk of human trafficking (roundtable)
summary_en: At a roundtable on recent human trafficking trends held at the Prothom Alo office on Tuesday (about 16 July 2024), organised by Winrock International's Ashshash project with the Swiss embassy, speakers said traffickers now misuse technology such as TikTok and that climate change adds to the risk. facts.statement: RMMRU executive director Professor C R Abrar said human trafficking can also occur within the labour migration process, which the government does not acknowledge; many workers in various countries live like slaves, and workers who returned during Covid had been trafficking victims although they went abroad with government clearance.

facts.source_in_article: A K M Masud Ali, INCIDIN Bangladesh

facts.statement: Shariful Hasan, associate director (Migration Programme and Youth Platform) of BRAC, said Bangladesh is first among the countries whose people go abroad by crossing the Mediterranean, and that people lack a clear idea of trafficking and safe migration.

Salma Ali, president of the Bangladesh National Woman Lawyers' Association, said laws and rules against trafficking exist but are not properly applied, the masterminds stay out of reach, and victims and witnesses have no protection.
Tariqul Islam, country director of Justice and Care, said that in cross-border trafficking the two countries have different laws, so rescuing a victim takes a long time.

Dipta Rakshit, Winrock International's country representative and Ashshash project director, said educated people too are now falling into the traps of traffickers of the 'TikTok Hridoy' type and that the pattern of trafficking has changed.

headline_en: Why are young Bangladeshi workers dying in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: Based on a Guardian investigation, the article reports that at least 13,685 Bangladeshi workers died in Saudi Arabia in 2008-2022, including 1,502 in 2022, and that most deaths are recorded as 'natural' without post-mortem, leaving families with no explanation and no compensation. It tells the case of Abdul Jalil Sheikh (35), who borrowed BDT 5 lakh to go and came back in a coffin within a year. The Saudi ministry denies negligence; BRAC's Shariful Hasan calls for the causes of death to be investigated.

facts.statement: According to Bangladesh government data, at least 13,685 Bangladeshi workers died in Saudi Arabia in the 14 years 2008-2022, of whom 1,502 died in 2022 alone, an average of more than four a day.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh government data, cited from the Guardian

facts.statement: The average age of Bangladeshi workers whose deaths in Saudi Arabia in 2022 were recorded as 'natural' was 44, against a male life expectancy of 71 in Bangladesh. Based on Saudi documents, Bangladesh authorities recorded 76 percent of Bangladeshis who died between January and October 2022 as 'natural' deaths.

The Guardian found that in most cases the cause of death is not explained: Saudi death certificates say 'natural causes', 'heart problem' or 'respiratory problem', and as a result no post-mortem is initiated to identify the cause.
The slip attached to Abdul Jalil Sheikh's coffin read: 'Cause of death: natural. Post-mortem: not requested. Compensation: none.' His relatives will get no compensation from Saudi Arabia.

UK-based rights group FairSquare says the cause of death goes unexplained in more than 50 percent of deaths of migrant workers in Gulf countries; rights groups say harsh work and living conditions, exploitation, stress and heatstroke may contribute to the death rate.

Amnesty International says migrant workers in Saudi Arabia are treated terribly, face exploitation and abuse because of the 'sponsorship system', and are sometimes forcibly confined in inhuman conditions or forcibly sent home.

Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development said in a statement that it is committed to a safe working environment for all migrant workers including more than 2.5 million Bangladeshi workers, that post-mortems are done where required, that death certificates are issued transparently and that no case of negligence had been found. Bangladesh authorities and FIFA declined to comment to the Guardian.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development statement

facts.statement: Shariful Hasan of BRAC's migration programme said Bangladeshi workers can go to Saudi Arabia only after a medical test at health centres designated by the Saudi authorities, meaning they are physically fit when they go; he said both governments must investigate the causes of death and warned deaths could rise if Saudi Arabia hosts the 2034 World Cup.
facts.source_in_article: Shariful Hasan, associate director, BRAC migration programme

facts.statement: The article states that Jalil was one of about 50,000 (as printed: 'প্রায় ৫০ হাজার') workers who went from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia in 2023.

headline_en: Over 2.4 million workers went abroad in 2 years but remittances barely rose
summary_en: More than 2.4 million workers went abroad in 2022 and 2023, both record years, yet remittances in 2023 were USD 21.91 billion, only USD 620 million above 2022 and below 2021. Experts blame hundi and money laundering, a wide gap between bank and informal dollar rates, and workers who find no job abroad. Wage Earners' Welfare Board data show 86,621 migrants came back empty-handed on embassy out passes in 2023, and an RMMRU survey of 218 returnees found 15 percent got no work.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh by calendar year (Bangladesh Bank and BMET data): USD 15.54 billion in 2018, 18.35 billion in 2019, 21.75 billion in 2020, 22.07 billion in 2021 (the record), 21.29 billion in 2022 and 21.91 billion in 2023.

BMET data: more than 1 million workers went abroad in a year for the first time in 2017; over 700,000 in 2019; about 200,000 in 2020; over 600,000 in 2021; more than 1,135,000 in 2022; and more than 1.3 million in 2023, the record.
Migration experts say it usually takes a new worker six months to a year after going abroad to start sending money home.

In late December 2023 migrants sending money through legal channels received BDT 109.50 per US dollar (it was BDT 110.50 a month and a half earlier), plus a 2.5 percent government incentive and an equal incentive from banks; some banks were said to be buying remittances at BDT 123, and hundi rings paid still more.

Those concerned say hundi rings abroad buy dollars from migrants to assist money laundering and deliver taka to the migrant's family through domestic groups; there are also allegations that Bangladeshi-owned money exchange and remittance companies are involved in money laundering.

A recent study by North South University's Center for Migration Studies (CMS) found that hundi dealers' networks reach remote areas, promise quick and cheap transfers, and if a migrant cannot send money in a month they lend and send the money home on their own initiative, to be repaid next month; migrants who went abroad on loans at high cost choose whichever channel gives the highest exchange rate to repay debt fast.
facts.source_in_article: Center for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Migrants who return having lost everything or after being detained by police abroad have no passport; the embassy gives them an 'out pass' (a legal travel permit) to return, and only returnees on out passes are counted by the government. Those who return with passports are not counted.

Wage Earners' Welfare Board data show 86,621 migrants returned to Bangladesh empty-handed in 2023: 83,719 men and 2,902 women. Sector insiders say the true number of failed migrations exceeds 100,000 a year.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board; migration sector insiders

facts.statement: An RMMRU survey of 218 returned migrants found 15 percent got no work at all abroad and 20 percent did not get work as per contract; 15 percent returned within one month of going and 29 percent within six months, falling into debt.
The World Bank and KNOMAD Migration and Development Brief 39 forecast Bangladesh's formal remittances at USD 23 billion for 2023; actual receipts were about USD 1 billion less.
Recruiting agency owners say that, lacking a legal way to send money abroad, agency owners also use hundi for the visa trade.

Migration expert Asif Munier said skilled workers from other countries are going for the kinds of jobs Bangladeshis go for, so demand for Bangladeshi workers is falling, they cannot earn more, and many do not get regular work. Former World Bank Dhaka lead economist Zahid Hussain said the widening gap between formal and informal dollar rates pushes migrants to hundi.

headline_en: Tests begin for workers wishing to go to DHL in Malaysia at no cost
summary_en: DHL Supply Chain in Malaysia is taking Bangladeshi workers at zero migration cost through state-owned BOESL. From 4,029 online applicants, 300 were shortlisted by electronic lottery on 8 November 2026, and a nine-member Malaysian delegation began practical tests and interviews on Thursday 12 November to pick 112. The ministry says 10,000 workers will be sent in phases at no cost, and BOESL warned candidates against any payment to brokers.

facts.statement: Malaysia's DHL Supply Chain company will take workers from Bangladesh at zero migration cost; 10,000 workers are to be sent in phases at no cost, with state recruiting agency BOESL handling the sending.

Online applications were accepted from 6 November until 4 pm on 8 November 2026; 4,029 candidates applied and 300 were chosen in a preliminary electronic lottery on 8 November: 200 for Operations Assistant and 100 for Technical Skill Workers. The list was published on BOESL's official website and Facebook page.

A nine-member delegation from Malaysia is holding in-person practical tests and interviews from Thursday 12 November to 15 November 2026 to finally select 112 workers from the 300, checking professional skill, practical ability and suitability for the post.
BOESL says it does not interfere in the selection and the candidates chosen by the employer are final.

facts.statement: BOESL managing director Mohammad Rashedul Haque said that if any broker, middleman or unauthorised person tries to take money at any stage of recruitment, or any candidate engages in an unethical transaction, strict legal action will be taken against both on proof; he specially asked candidates to refrain from any financial transaction.

headline_en: Skills-based education for the goal of a trillion-dollar economy
summary_en: An article by Dhaka University IBA professor Md. Ridwanul Haque argues Bangladesh must build skilled workers to meet rising global demand for nurses, electricians, plumbers and care workers. BMET data show that of about 1,128,000 workers who went abroad in 2025, 43.47 percent were less-skilled and 34.46 percent semi-skilled. Japan aimed to take about 820,000 foreign skilled workers in 16 sectors by March 2029, but Bangladesh's planned sending under its MoU with NBCC is only 2,000, 6,000 and 18,000 in 2026-2028.

facts.statement: BMET data: about 1,128,000 workers went abroad from Bangladesh in 2025; 43.47 percent were less-skilled, 34.46 percent semi-skilled, 19.13 percent skilled and 2.94 percent professionals. Only 5.5 percent of outbound workers in 2025 were women.

Japan set a target of taking about 820,000 foreign skilled workers in 16 sectors by March 2029, including construction, industrial manufacturing, agriculture, food processing and elderly care; the article notes the target may be revised by later policy changes.

The memorandum of understanding with NBCC (described as a Japanese business association) aims to send 100,000 Bangladeshi workers in five years, but the recruitment plan for 2026, 2027 and 2028 is 2,000, 6,000 and 18,000 respectively; the government's own target is to send 50,000 workers to Japan by 2030.

To work in Japan technical skill alone is not enough: in many occupations one must pass Japanese language and specific skills tests. In Germany and other European countries, language and recognition of professional qualifications are also important.
By NBCC's estimate, Japan may need more than 400,000 nursing-care workers in the coming years; the author says there is employment potential in this sector for Bangladeshi women too.

A 2025 WHO report says the world was short of about 5.8 million nurses in 2023, which may fall to 4.1 million in 2030. Australia, New Zealand and Germany have demand for electricians, plumbers, welders, carpenters and air-conditioning technicians.
Remittances to Bangladesh reached a record USD 35.56 billion in fiscal year 2025-26.
The government's 2026-27 budget announced phased introduction of technical education from class six and allocated BDT 18,457 crore to the Technical and Madrasah Education Division.

The author says less-skilled workers face low wages, limited career progress and more workplace risk, and suggests training plans aimed at elderly care, construction and food processing for Japan, nursing and technical trades for Europe, and upskilling existing workers for the Middle East, with foreign language teaching attached.

headline_en: 35 Bangladeshis sent back from Italy, Greece and Cyprus
summary_en: Three European countries returned 35 Bangladeshis on a chartered special flight that landed in Dhaka at 8:15 am on Friday 23 October 2026: 19 from Italy, 10 from Greece and 6 from Cyprus. BRAC's migration programme gave them emergency help, counselling and money to reach home at the airport under the EU and BRAC funded Prottasha-2 project. About 5,000 Bangladeshis have been returned under the 2017 SOP agreement with European countries.

facts.statement: 35 Bangladeshis were sent back from Europe on a chartered special flight (PVG 9445) that landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at 8:15 am on Friday 23 October 2026: 19 from Italy, 10 from Greece and 6 from Cyprus.

At the airport, with the cooperation of Civil Aviation Security and the Probashi Kallyan (expatriates' welfare) Desk, BRAC's migration programme gave the returnees emergency assistance, counselling and financial help to reach their homes, under the Prottasha-2 project jointly funded by the European Union and BRAC; economic support is to be given to all after later counselling and training.
The Bangladesh government signed a Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) agreement with European countries in 2017 for bringing back undocumented or irregular Bangladeshis from Europe.

About 5,000 Bangladeshis have come back under the SOP so far, the most from Cyprus, Italy, Romania and France. BRAC's Shariful Hasan said that in the past few years the largest numbers of returnees from Europe that BRAC received were from Italy, Greece and Germany.
Shariful Hasan said awareness work is under way across Bangladesh so people do not take risks to go to Europe, and the government has stepped up initiatives to send workers to Europe legally.

headline_en: Women workers going abroad rising slightly; destinations depend on two countries
summary_en: In the first eight months of 2026 more than 42,000 Bangladeshi women went to work in 48 countries, over 90 percent of them to Saudi Arabia and Jordan. Women's overseas employment fell from 105,466 in 2022 to 62,317 in 2025, and returnees report beatings, sexual abuse, work in several houses, 14 to 16 hour days and unpaid wages. The state minister says legal aid has been started in 13 countries and a safe home runs in Saudi Arabia; NGOs say women should not go unless safety is ensured.

facts.statement: In the first eight months of 2026 more than 42,000 women workers went from Bangladesh to 48 countries; more than 90 percent went to just two countries, Saudi Arabia and Jordan. This was 5,214 more, or about 14 percent more, than in the same period of 2025.

BMET data: 105,466 women workers went abroad in 2022 and 62,317 in 2025, a fall of about 41 percent in three years. More than 100,000 women a year went abroad for five straight years from 2015 to 2019; the number fell in 2020 with Covid, rose in the next two years and fell again in 2023.

Many returning women workers allege physical and mental torture, sexual abuse, being made to work in several houses, long hours, and not getting proper wages or food. NGO officials list being taken on false promises, 14 to 16 hour workdays, low and irregular pay and irregular food; there have been suicides, and some who ran away came home after being detained by police.
facts.source_in_article: Returnee women; officials of BRAC, RMMRU, OKUP and Nari Sramik Kendra

facts.statement: Returnee Anjana of Manikganj said a recruiting agency gets money for each woman worker it sends to Saudi Arabia, so the agency profits just by sending and sends women without a job.

State minister for expatriates' welfare Md. Nurul Haque said legal aid has been started in 13 countries and a safe home is running in Saudi Arabia, which he said has reduced abuse; caregiver and housekeeping training is given at technical training centres, and the government is looking at skilled markets such as Japan and Hong Kong.

An OKUP study in 2025 found that 94 percent of women workers forced to return had suffered regular physical and mental abuse abroad, 47 percent had suffered sexual harassment, and 82 percent had to work from dawn to midnight.

Sumaiya Islam, executive director of Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra, said women are taken on the promise of one job and made to do several, there are allegations of sexual abuse, and it is better for women not to go if safety is not ensured.
facts.source_in_article: Sumaiya Islam, Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra

facts.statement: Migration sector people say women going abroad do not know the language and have no training in cooking or housework, employers (kafeel) make them work in several homes and abuse them, and Saudi Arabia is turning to alternative sources, taking workers from African countries.

BRAC, from experience in 42 countries, says Nepal, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam are far ahead in protecting their citizens and have stopped sending workers when needed, which Bangladesh has not done. OKUP says that in Charbhadrasan, Faridpur, women went abroad from almost every household but no longer want to go; men are going instead.
OKUP chairperson Shakirul Islam said abused women workers return and get no justice even when harmed, others have become aware, and no good market or variety of work has been created for women.

headline_en: About 100 migrants including Bangladeshis detained at the Croatia border
summary_en: Bosnian border police detained about 100 migrants from three countries, mostly Bangladeshis, in two operations on Wednesday 2 September 2026 at Bistrica in northern Bosnia as they tried to enter EU member Croatia. The first group of 63 had 23 Bangladeshis and 40 Pakistanis; a second group of 33 included Bangladeshis, Afghans and Pakistanis. They were preparing to cross the Sava river in two boats; Frontex recorded over 4,900 irregular crossings on the Balkan route in the first seven months of 2026.

facts.statement: Bosnian border police detained about 100 migrants in two separate operations on Wednesday 2 September 2026 at the border in the Bistrica area of northern Bosnia as they tried to enter Croatia; police said a large share were Bangladeshi. The first group of 63 comprised 23 Bangladeshis and 40 Pakistanis; the second group of 33 included nationals of Bangladesh, Afghanistan and Pakistan (number of Bangladeshis not specified).

The migrants were preparing to use two boats to cross the border river Sava from Bosnia into Croatia; police seized the boats and identified two suspected human smugglers. Irregular migrants regularly use the Balkan route into Europe, with Bosnia as a transit country.

According to EU border agency Frontex, more than 4,900 irregular border crossings were registered on the Balkan route in the first seven months of 2026, 26 percent fewer than in the same period of 2025.
